apush-saq-0025.a: Spain built missions to bring Native peoples into the mission system, teaching Christianity and Spanish ways; missions let the Crown hold Florida with few soldiers.
apush-saq-0025.b: The mission system pressed the Guale to live under Spanish priests and follow Christian teaching, replacing their own religious practices and putting daily life under Spanish control.
apush-saq-0025.c: The Guale answered with Juanillo's Revolt in 1597, killing several missionaries - violent resistance when autonomy was threatened.

apush-saq-0026.a: Cortes cast the idols down the temple steps and put up images of the Virgin and the saints.
apush-saq-0026.b: They believed their idols bestowed all temporal good and would be angry and withhold their gifts if ill-treated; they feared the people would rise against Cortes.
apush-saq-0026.c: It shows the Spanish aimed to replace Native religion with Christianity and present conquest as a religious mission - justifying war to the king.

apush-saq-0027.a: Bartolome de las Casas, a Dominican friar, seated at a writing desk with a quill.
apush-saq-0027.b: The portrait was engraved in 1791, more than two centuries after Las Casas died in 1566, so it is an idealized imagining, not drawn from life.
apush-saq-0027.c: His 1542 account of Spanish cruelty was translated and printed by Spain's Protestant rivals, spreading the Black Legend and fueling European debate about whether the conquest was just and whether Native peoples had rights.

apush-saq-0028.a: African songs sung in the fields (also voodoo, mixing Christianity with African beliefs).
apush-saq-0028.b: Enslaved people blended the language and religion of their masters with ancestral traditions - e.g. voodoo mixed Christianity with African beliefs.
apush-saq-0028.c: Maroon communities were enclaves apart from the plantation where African traditions could be kept alive.

apush-saq-0029.a: Some peoples were by nature slaves, fit to be ruled by others; the Spanish had the right and duty to conquer and Christianize them.
apush-saq-0029.b: Aristotle - the claim that some peoples are natural slaves.
apush-saq-0029.c: Las Casas answered from natural law: Native peoples were rational human beings with rights, and only peaceful preaching could justify Spanish rule.

apush-saq-0030.a: Florida Indians planting beans and maize - women carrying baskets of seed, men digging with hoes in rows across a cleared field.
apush-saq-0030.b: Native peoples farmed intensively and in an organized way - maize and beans in rows, with a gendered division of labor.
apush-saq-0030.c: De Bry never visited Florida; he worked from Le Moyne's drawings and gave the figures European features, so the image is a European imagining, not a direct record.

apush-saq-0031.a: American silver drove prices up in Spain and across Europe - inflation.
apush-saq-0031.b: The crown spent the silver on armies, wars, and interest rather than investing in farms or workshops; a tiny landowning class saw no reason to modernize, so the wealth passed through Spain.
apush-saq-0031.c: Silver set off a long wave of inflation across Western Europe; it also funded an arms race as Spain's large army forced rivals to multiply their forces.

apush-saq-0032.a: Columbus saw the Taino as gentle, unarmed people who would make fine servants; he believed fifty men could subjugate them all.
apush-saq-0032.b: From the first landing, the Spanish aimed to rule Native peoples and put them to work, judging them by their usefulness as subjects and servants.
apush-saq-0032.c: The entry survives only in a copy made by Las Casas decades later, so the words may not be exactly Columbus's; Columbus was also writing to justify his voyage to the crown.

apush-saq-0033.a: Hispaniola fell from over 1,000,000 people in 1492 to about 500 by the 1540s - a near-total collapse; across the Americas populations fell 50 to 90 percent between 1500 and 1650.
apush-saq-0033.b: Disease - smallpox and other Old World diseases struck peoples with no immunity; war, slavery, and broken food systems helped the dying along.
apush-saq-0033.c: As Native labor died off, the Spanish had to find new labor, turning increasingly to enslaved Africans.

apush-leq-0009.thesis: European cultural practices transformed Native American societies to a great extent - missions, conversion, intermarriage and mestizo populations, and new labor systems remade daily life, religion, and social order - though Native peoples also resisted and adapted, so the transformation was not total.

apush-leq-0010.thesis: Spanish and French interactions differed to a great extent: Spain built an empire of mines, missions, and coerced labor, while France built fur-trade partnerships and alliances - though both crowns wanted wealth and took Native land.
evidence: intermarriage patterns: Spanish mestizos vs English whole families

apush-leq-0011.thesis: Disease was the most significant cause of Spanish success to a great extent: smallpox at Tenochtitlan in 1520 killed defenders including Cuitlahuac, and the 50-90% population decline hollowed out resistance - though steel, horses, and Native allies (Tlaxcalans) also mattered, so disease led but did not work alone.
evidence: no immunity after thousands of years apart
Tlaxcalan allies and steel/horses as secondary factors
